# Numbering figures and tables

A reviewer who writes "the second survival curve in the eligibility section"
has already lost a minute finding it; one who writes "Figure 5.2" has not.
Quarto will number every figure and table in a report or a book, and keep the
numbers right as chapters grow, but only for the ones it recognizes. This
recipe is about making sure it recognizes all of them.

## When to use it

Always, in anything longer than a page that someone will read and discuss: an
analysis report for co-authors, a research notebook, a job built from an
`hvtiRtemplates` template. A figure without a number cannot be cited in a
comment, a slide, or an email, and a table caption that prints without a
number looks finished when it is not.

## The rule

Quarto numbers a figure when its chunk label starts with `fig-` **and** the
chunk has a `fig-cap`, and a table when its label starts with `tbl-` and the
chunk has a `tbl-cap`. The labels and captions are the `#|` option lines at
the top of each chunk. Both halves matter. A caption alone prints, unnumbered,
and a `fig-` label with no caption is not numbered either.

```r
#| label: fig-km-repair
#| fig-cap: "Freedom from death or transplant by repair, with the number at risk."
plot(km)
```

```r
#| label: tbl-cohort
#| tbl-cap: "Preoperative characteristics by repair: median (15th, 85th percentile) or n (%)."
knitr::kable(cohort_table)
```

Refer to them as `@fig-km-repair` and `@tbl-cohort`; Quarto writes "Figure
2.1" and "Table 3.4" and links to them. In a book the chapter number comes
first, so renumbering a chapter renumbers its figures without your help.

## Table captions go in `tbl-cap`

`knitr::kable(caption = "...")` is the habit most of us bring from R Markdown,
and it still prints a caption. But Quarto does not see it as a table caption,
so the table gets no number and `@tbl-` cannot reach it. Move the text into
`tbl-cap` and drop the argument; leaving both prints the caption twice. A
caption built from data works too:

```r
#| label: tbl-designs
#| tbl-cap: !expr paste0("The four designs. ", primary_design, " is the primary analysis.")
knitr::kable(designs)
```

The objects the expression uses must exist before the chunk runs, so compute
them in an earlier chunk.

## One output, one chunk

A chunk carries one label, so it can carry one number. A chunk that prints a
table and then a figure needs splitting into two, each with its own label and
caption; keep the shared computation and any file writes in the first. The
exception is a chunk whose `kable()` calls are alternatives, an `if`/`else`
that prints one table or the other: it still shows one table and keeps one
label.

## A figure per item

The awkward case is a loop that draws one figure per variable, say a
partial-dependence figure for each predictor a forest selected. One chunk
cannot label twenty figures. Instead, build the plots in the loop and emit
each one as its own child chunk with `knitr::knit_child()`, inside a chunk
with `results: asis`:

```r
#| results: asis
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(keys))   # each key becomes a label; two alike would collide
fence <- strrep("`", 3)
children <- vapply(seq_along(plots), function(i) knitr::knit_child(text = paste(c(
  paste0("\n\n#### ", headings[i], "\n"),
  paste0(fence, "{r}"),
  paste0("#| label: fig-partial-", keys[i]),
  paste0('#| fig-cap: "', headings[i], ': partial dependence."'),
  sprintf("print(plots[[%d]])", i),
  fence, ""), collapse = "\n"), envir = environment(), quiet = TRUE), character(1))
cat(children, sep = "\n")
```

Each figure gets its heading, its number and a label you can cite
(`@fig-partial-lv-size`). The keys go into labels, so keep them to lowercase
letters, digits and hyphens; the `stopifnot()` at the top halts the render
if two collide, rather than letting `@fig-` point at the wrong figure. The fence is built with
`strrep()` so that the three backticks inside the chunk do not close it early.

## Where the caption sits

Quarto puts a figure's caption below it and a table's caption above it, and we
keep those defaults. They are the journals' convention too: a table's title
is read before its rows, and a figure's legend after the picture. The house
JTCVS table export, `hvtiRtables::hv_man_table_save_jtcvs()` (see [Manuscript
tables](hv_tables.qmd)), puts the bold caption above the table for
the same reason.

## Pitfalls

- **A caption with no number.** The caption is there, so the figure looks
  done. Check the rendered page for "Figure" in front of the caption, or let a
  test check the source (below).
- **A rename that breaks a test.** Renaming `km-repair` to `fig-km-repair` is
  harmless to Quarto, but a test that extracts the chunk by its label will no
  longer find it. Search the tests before renaming.
- **A `fig-` chunk that draws nothing.** Quarto expects a figure from a
  `fig-` chunk. A chunk that only fits a model or prints a summary is not a
  figure; leave it unlabelled.
- **Hand-written numbers.** "As Figure 3 shows" goes stale the first time a
  figure is added above it. Write `@fig-...` and let Quarto count.

`hvtiRtemplates` checks every template against this rule in
`test-template-numbering.R`, so a job built from a template starts numbered.
